panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A is an X-ray showing apposition of spinous processes, a direct sign of Baastrup disease as described in the caption and vocabulary. B: Panel B is a CT scan showing hyperostosis and osteosclerosis of the spinous processes, characteristic of sclerosis in Baastrup disease. C: Panel C is an MRI showing high T2 signal around the spinous processes, indicative of inflammation or fluid, consistent with Baastrup disease.

The focal midline back pain was directly reproduced by palpation over the spinous processes, but no tenderness was observed upon palpation of the lumbar facet joints. Profile views of X‐ray examinations at upright neutral, flexion, and extension positions were performed. Hyperostosis and osteosclerosis of the spinous processes were evaluated by CT. MRI was performed to evaluate edema and inflammation of the interspinous ligaments in fat‐suppressed T2‐weighted images (Fig. 1). Details of the patients' clinical characteristics and pain scores are shown in Table 1.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A is an MRI T1 weighted image demonstrating the sclerotic and hypertrophic 'kissings' of the spinous processes from L2 to L5, a characteristic radiological finding of Baastrup disease. B: Panel B is an MRI T2 weighted image demonstrating the hypertrophic 'kissings' of the spinous processes and mild facet hypertrophy, consistent with Baastrup disease findings described in the caption.

in_text_mentions: MRI corroborated these findings, with sclerotic and hypertrophic “kissing” spinous processes from L2 to L5, with mild L5-S1 facet hypertrophy (Figure 2). There was no significant spinal canal or neural foraminal stenosis. The patient was treated with steroid injections under fluoroscopic guidance with marked symptomatic relief.

in_text_mentions: plaints of a sore back that worsened with extension and arching. Upon physical examination, there was pain to palpation along her thoracic spinous processes and adjacent thoracic paraspinal muscles. Upon neurological examination, the patient had no focal neurological deficits and negative provocative exam maneuvers (Spurling’s). The first thoracic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in February 2014 appeared normal; however, a repeat thoracic MRI in September 2014 showed early suspicion for spinous process abnormality at the thoracolumbar junction region vertebra, particularly T12 (see Figure 1).

plate_findings.evidence: prominent, hypertrophic spinous processes, contacting one another

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: The panel is a plain film radiograph clearly depicting hypertrophic, contacting spinous processes and adjacent sclerosis, consistent with Baastrup's disease. B: The panel is a CT scan image illustrating the structural changes (hypertrophy and sclerosis) associated with Baastrup's disease as described in the caption. C: The panel is a cross-sectional CT image showing the bony changes characteristic of Baastrup's disease as described in the text.

in_text_mentions: Ultimately, imaging studies confirmed our clinical suspicion. CT scan revealed mild, lumbar spondylosis with prominent and hypertrophic spinous processes that were touching each other with adjacent sclerosis (Figure 1).
